rows.question: Best industry for the quickest gains
problems: no Bonds / Broad market building block in ['Information Technology']
rows.answer:
## Summary

- Recommended group: Information Technology, which fits Amira's interest in AI/emerging tech; because her profile needs at least 3 asset classes, pair it with a Bonds or Broad market building block [fact: step 20, 2].
- Main risk: Information Technology's annualized volatility is 30.1%, with a -43.9% drawdown in the 2022 stress test — high but consistent with Amira's high risk tolerance and 15+ year horizon [fact: step 11, 14].
- No sector reliably gives "quickest gains"; past 6-month momentum (basket +27.8%) and 5-year returns describe history only, not future results [fact: step 16, 11] [assumption].

## Recommendation

For Amira's profile, Information Technology is the strongest match among the four candidates compared: it shows the highest 5-year total return (+177.6%, annualized 23.3%) versus Consumer Discretionary (+80.1%), Communication Services (+130.1%), and Industrials (+24.2%) [fact: step 11, 7, 9, 10]. It also directly matches her stated interest in AI/emerging tech through names like NVDA, MSFT, AAPL [fact: step 2]. Because her profile requires at least 3 asset classes, Information Technology should be paired with a building block such as Bonds or Broad market, taken from the list_sectors step [fact: step 2]. Note: no sector can promise "quickest gains" — what the data shows is past momentum and returns, not a prediction [assumption].

## Why it fits

- Annualized volatility 30.1%, max drawdown -45.8%, and a -43.9% drop in the 2022 stress test show "Very High" risk, matching Amira's high risk tolerance and long horizon [fact: step 11, 14].
- 6-month momentum of +27.8% and trading above its 200-day average suggest recent strength, though NVDA individually is below its 200-day average and down -12.5% over 12 months [fact: step 16].
- Mid-cycle phase tilts historically favor Information Technology, Industrials, and Communication Services, though rising credit-spread stress (+0.49 points over 3 months) and weakening consumer sentiment (-7.0 points over 12 months) add macro risk [fact: step 3, 4] [assumption].

## Profile check

- Crypto cap: pass, 0.0% vs 15.0% limit [fact: step 20].
- Sector cap: info only — keep at most 50.0% of the portfolio in Information Technology (no weight proposed yet) [fact: step 20].
- Minimum asset classes: info — target covers only 1 asset class; portfolio needs at least 3, so pairing is needed [fact: step 20].

## Example assets

SHOP.TO (Shopify), CSU.TO (Constellation Software), AAPL (Apple), MSFT (Microsoft), NVDA (NVIDIA) [fact: step 2].

## Market context

Historically, in a mid-cycle phase, sectors like Information Technology, Industrials, and Communication Services have tended to do relatively well; VIX is at a "normal" mood level of 18.7 while credit spreads have been rising [fact: step 3, 4] [assumption].

## What could go wrong / limitations

Volatility of 30.1% and a -45.8% max drawdown mean large swings are possible [fact: step 11]. The sector basket mixes five single stocks at equal weight, rebalanced daily, with data limited to common trading dates only [fact: step 11]. Single-name volatility inside the basket varies widely, e.g., NVDA at 51.4% [fact: step 11].

_Educational simulation for a fictional persona (Amira). Not personalized financial advice._

rows.question: I want to put a big part of my savings in NVDA, good idea?
rows.answer:

- Recommended: Consumer Staples (ATD.TO, PG), paired with Bonds to help meet Robert's 50.0% bonds/cash minimum [fact: step 10, 12].
- Main risk: Consumer Staples' 17.0% annualized volatility still exceeds Robert's 10.0% limit, so it fits only as a small, defensive sleeve for a low-moderate-risk, capital-preservation investor [fact: step 10].

## Recommendation
Putting a big part of Robert's savings into NVDA is not suitable: it conflicts with his hard 10.0% single-stock cap (proposed 50.0%) and flags on both volatility (51.1% vs 10.0%) and the 2022 stress test (-59.2% vs -15.0%) [fact: step 7]. The Information Technology sector that contains NVDA also flags on volatility (30.1%) and 2022 drawdown (-43.9%), so it is not a workaround [fact: step 11]. Instead, Consumer Staples (ATD.TO, PG) fits better, paired with Bonds to work toward Robert's 50.0% bonds/cash minimum [fact: step 10, 12].

## Why it fits
- Consumer Staples passed the 2022 stress test at -13.7% vs a -15.0% limit, with positive 12-month momentum of +19.0% and price above its 200-day average [fact: step 10, 13].
- It still flags on volatility, 17.0% vs Robert's 10.0% limit, so it should stay a smaller slice, not a core bet [fact: step 10].
- Within Bonds, ZST.TO (0.6% vol, -0.4% 2022 drawdown) and AGG (7.4% vol, -10.7% drawdown) pass Robert's limits individually, while TLT (16.1% vol, -31.8% drawdown) does not [fact: step 12].

## Profile check
- NVDA: conflict on single-stock cap (50.0% vs 10.0%); flags on volatility (51.1% vs 10.0%) and 2022 drawdown (-59.2% vs -15.0%); info that 50.0% bonds/cash minimum still applies [fact: step 7].
- Consumer Staples: flag on volatility (17.0% vs 10.0%); pass on 2022 drawdown (-13.7% vs -15.0%); info on bonds/cash minimum [fact: step 10].
- Bonds: pass on bonds/cash minimum; flag on volatility and 2022 drawdown for XBB.TO/TLT, but ZST.TO and AGG pass both individually [fact: step 12].

## Example assets
Consumer Staples: ATD.TO (Alimentation Couche-Tard), PG (Procter & Gamble) [fact: step 2]. Bonds: XBB.TO, ZST.TO, AGG, TLT [fact: step 2].

## Market context
Mid-cycle phase, historically sectors like Information Technology, Industrials and Communication Services have tended to do relatively well [assumption: step 3]. Mood is normal on the VIX (18.7) but credit spreads have risen 0.49 points over 3 months, a stress signal [assumption: step 4].

## What could go wrong / limitations
Consumer Staples and Health Care/Utilities checks use a 1- or 2-asset basket, not diversified [fact: step 8, 9, 10]. The Bonds and NVDA sector checks warn of fixed 2022 windows and equal-weight, common-dates-only baskets [fact: step 6, 10, 12]. Past returns and momentum describe history only; no sector reliably gives quick gains, and any choice should stay within Robert's 3-5 year horizon.

rows.question: Which industry gives balanced growth for me?
rows.answer:

- Main risk: Utilities' annualized volatility is 14.7%, just under Mateo's 15.0% limit, fitting his moderate risk tolerance and 8–12 year horizon [fact: step 5].

## Recommendation

For Mateo's moderate, ESG-focused, low-speculation profile, **Utilities** is the industry that best fits "balanced growth" [fact: step 5, 20]. The mid-cycle tilt favors Information Technology, Industrials and Communication Services historically [fact: step 3], but those (and Financials, Consumer Staples, Health Care) all flag against Mateo's 15.0% volatility limit on their own (19.9%–30.1%) [fact: step 6, 10, 14, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23, 25], so chasing the cycle tilt would push past his limits — the request to simply follow the "hot" sectors is challenged here. Energy is excluded: it flags on volatility (20.5%) and holds all three of Mateo's ESG-review tickers (ENB.TO, CNQ.TO, XOM) [fact: step 24]. Because Mateo has a 30.0% bonds minimum, pair Utilities with the **Bonds** building block, using XBB.TO, ZST.TO or AGG rather than TLT, since TLT alone breaches the 15.0% volatility limit (16.1%) [fact: step 26].

## Why it fits
- Volatility 14.7%, within the 15.0% limit [fact: step 5].
- 2022 stress test: -7.9% return, -24.0% max drawdown — moderate behavior in a down year [fact: step 11].
- 12-month momentum +18.4%, trading above its 200-day average [fact: step 27].
- No ESG-review names in Utilities, matching Mateo's ESG preference [fact: step 20].

- Bonds: volatility flag only for TLT (16.1% vs 15.0% limit); XBB.TO, ZST.TO, AGG stay within it; bonds minimum satisfied; no ESG-review names [fact: step 26].

- Bonds: XBB.TO (iShares Core Canadian Universe Bond Index ETF), ZST.TO (BMO Ultra Short-Term Bond ETF), AGG (iShares Core U.S. Aggregate Bond ETF) [fact: step 2].

## Market context

## What could go wrong / limitations
- Utilities is represented by one asset (FTS.TO), so it is not diversified [fact: step 5]. Bonds are reported member-by-member with no blended figure [fact: step 15]. Past returns and momentum describe history only; no sector reliably gives quick or guaranteed gains, and Mateo's 8-12 year horizon should guide pacing, not short-term momentum [fact: step 27].
